<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, TeslaMate is a self-hosted data logger for Tesla vehicles. It is built with Elixir (using the Phoenix framework for its web interface) and relies on a Postgres database for storing vehicle and drive data. Data is both ingested from the Tesla API and external CSV importers (e.g., TeslaFi) and then published to external systems via MQTT and visualized using Grafana dashboards. Here’s how you can create a detailed system design/architecture diagram tailored to this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Core Application (TeslaMate Engine): Represent the heart of the system where the business logic lives. This includes modules for:
     - Tesla API integrations (see lib/tesla_api and its subdirectories for authentication, middleware, vehicle data processing, streaming, etc.).
     - Data import features (CSV importers under lib/teslamate/import).
     - Log and state management components (inside lib/teslamate/log and lib/teslamate/vehicles).
     - Application supervision and OTP lifecycle (modules like lib/teslamate/application.ex).

   • Web Interface: Built on the Phoenix framework:
     - Web controllers, live views, templates, and views (in lib/teslamate_web). This component handles the HTTP endpoint, real-time data display (live components), and admin interfaces.

   • Database (Postgres):
     - The Ecto repository (lib/teslamate/repo.ex) and related migration scripts (located in priv/repo/migrations) ensure that data is stored and maintained.
   
   • MQTT Integration:
     - Modules for publishing and subscribing to vehicle data (see lib/teslamate/mqtt and its submodules).
   
   • External Dashboard/Visualization:
     - Grafana integration, including container configuration (instances in the grafana folder) and dashboards (JSON files under grafana/dashboards) that fetch data from the database or MQTT.

   • Assets & Website Documentation:
     - The assets directory contains CSS, JavaScript, and build scripts for the web client.
     - There is also a "website" folder that holds documentation, guides, and other static content (used to showcase screenshots and integration instructions).

2. Map Out Relationships and Interactions:
   • Data Flow from Tesla Vehicles to Persistence:
     - The Tesla API module connects to Tesla endpoints or subscribed stream data.
     - Incoming vehicle data is managed by the TeslaMate core modules and stored into the Postgres database via the Ecto repo.
   
   • User Interaction via the Web Interface:
     - Users connect to the dashboard served by the Phoenix application.
     - Web controllers query the database for drive reports, battery health, charging stats, etc., and render them via live views and templates.
   
   • External Integrations:
     - MQTT modules publish vehicle states to an MQTT broker, allowing integration with Home Assistant or Node-RED.
     - Grafana dashboards pull data either directly from the database or via data sources set up through the dashboards’ configuration, providing visual reports.

3. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   • Separation of Concerns: 
     - The clear separation between Tesla API integration, business logic, web serving, and data persistence (database layer).
   • Modular Structure:
     - Distinct subcomponents (tesla_api, teslamate, teslamate_web) each responsible for specific areas.
   • Reliability & Scalability:
     - The use of OTP’s supervision trees ensures that components (e.g., data streaming, MQTT handling) are resilient.
   • Extensibility:
     - MQTT and CSV importers are designed for easy integration with other systems.

4. Relevant Technologies & Tools:
   • Elixir & Phoenix – Main programming language and web framework.
   • Postgres – Relational database used with Ecto.
   • Grafana – Visualization platform.
   • MQTT Broker – For real-time messaging with external systems.
   • Docker & CI/CD (GitHub workflows, Dockerfiles) – For deployment and continuous integration.

5. Guidelines for Creating the Diagram:
   • Clearly label each component (e.g., “Tesla API Module”, “Business Logic”, “Web Server (Phoenix)”, “Postgres Database”, “MQTT Broker”, “Grafana Dashboard”).
   • Use directional arrows:
     - Show data flowing from the Tesla API to the business logic.
     - Indicate how parsed and processed data is sent to the database.
     - Represent pull requests by the Web Interface from the database.
     - Illustrate the MQTT Publisher sending data to a broker and external services consuming it.
     - A separate arrow can indicate Grafana’s polling or connection to the Postgres database.
   • Use different colors or shapes:
     - For example, use rectangles for microservices/components, cylinders for databases, and cloud symbols for external services.
   • Include supplementary labels:
     - Annotate arrows with “data ingestion”, “API response”, “MQTT publish”, “DB queries”, etc.

6. Tailoring to TeslaMate’s Specific Structure:
   • Focus on showing a multi-tier structure:
     - A frontend layer (Phoenix Web Interface along with static assets) that communicates with a backend application.
     - A robust backend with modules performing vehicle data ingestion, import, and logging.
     - Clearly display middleware connectors such as the MQTT publishing modules to show how data is forwarded to integrations (Home Assistant, Node-RED) and Grafana.
   • In a full-stack context, emphasize how the Phoenix framework separates concerns (controllers, live views, templates) and how the underlying OTP application (in lib/teslamate) drives the core business logic.
   • Make sure to highlight the strong coupling between the discrete layers (API integration, DB storage, web presentation, external messaging).

By following these guidelines, the final diagram should give a comprehensive view of the TeslaMate architecture, from the reception of real-time Tesla vehicle data through the processing pipelines, its storage in the Postgres database, and its delivery both via a dynamic web interface and external dashboards/integrations. This level of detail will help any principal software engineer understand the flow, modularity, and interactions between various components of this application.
</explanation>
